items.title: The New Supply Chain Risk Is Dependency
items.dek: The real resilience question is no longer how much capacity exists, but how many practical ways cargo can move when preferred routes stop behaving normally.
body: The question, “How much capacity is available?” is becoming increasingly irrelevant.

This week alone, logistics networks were dealing with severe port congestion in East Asia, new operational pressure around the Strait of Hormuz, and further restrictions at the Panama Canal. None of these situations mean the world has suddenly run out of ships, terminals, trucks or infrastructure. The problem is that too much cargo still depends on a relatively small number of routes, gateways and operating assumptions.

At Shanghai and Ningbo, successive typhoons have created vessel queues stretching several days. Global containership capacity waiting to berth reached about 4.31 million TEU, with Shanghai waiting times reported as high as 12 days at some terminals. A leading carrier has already omitted Shanghai calls on certain voyages to protect onward schedules.

With this year’s lower-than-expected rainfall, the Panama Canal Authority announced reduced daily transit capacity beginning in September. It has also been adjusting draft restrictions and its booking system as water conditions change. Access to the Canal is becoming more conditional, particularly for vessels without secured reservations.
Then there is the Strait of Hormuz. This week, Iran threatened penalties, detention and possible cargo confiscation against dozens of tankers it says violated its transit requirements.
These events look unrelated.
One is weather. One is water availability. One is geopolitics.
Operationally, however, they expose the same weakness.
Supply chains that run efficiently through preferred routes are often much less efficient when those routes stop behaving normally.
That changes how resilience should be measured.

A company may have three carriers, but if all three depend on the same transshipment hub, the diversification is mostly cosmetic. A shipper may have several suppliers, but if all of them export through the same congested gateway, the risk remains concentrated. If alternatives only become visible after the primary routing fails, they are contingency plans rather than real options.
The better question is not:
How much capacity do you have?
It is:
How many practical ways do you have to move your cargo?
That means looking beyond freight rates and transit times when planning important shipments.
Efficiency matters. None of this means abandoning it.
But the cheapest or fastest routing on a normal day is not necessarily the lowest-cost routing across the life of a shipment.
A supply chain with one perfect route is efficient. A supply chain with three workable routes is resilient.

items.title: Capacity Exists, But How Much Can I Use Now?
items.dek: The global container fleet is bigger than ever. Yet effective capacity is shrinking.
body: The global container fleet is bigger than ever. There are ships in the water, containers in circulation and terminals operating. Yet effective capacity is shrinking.

Current port congestion is a useful example. More than 4.3 million TEU of container capacity is reportedly waiting to berth worldwide, exceeding the absolute congestion peak seen during the pandemic. East Asia is carrying much of that pressure, with large queues at Shanghai and Ningbo. Vessel delays are increasingly measured in days rather than hours.

A 15,000-TEU vessel sitting outside a port is still technically part of the global fleet. But while it waits, the ship falls behind schedule. Its next port call moves. Containers miss connections. Equipment stays in the wrong place. Another service begins operating with less usable capacity.
One delay becomes several.

A major carrier has omitted a Shanghai call on one service after adverse weather affected the schedule, rerouting cargo to protect the onward rotation. That makes operational sense for the vessel, but the affected containers now require another solution.
What actually matters is usable capacity at the time and place where the cargo needs it.
Congestion, weather, security, equipment imbalance, missed connections and specialized cargo requirements all consume usable capacity.
The transportation asset does not have to disappear. It only has to stop being available when you need it.
The question, then, is not simply:
“How much capacity exists?”
It is:
“How much capacity can I actually use, reliably, right now?”

items.title: The Strait Isn't Closed. So Why Does It Still Feel Like It Is?
items.dek: The Strait of Hormuz is a reminder that reality is far more complex and that a trade lane does not need to close before the logistics network is disrupted.
body: The logistics industry often prefers binary answers. Is the port open or closed? Is the canal operating or not? Is the border letting cargo through?
The Strait of Hormuz is a reminder that reality is far more complex and that a trade lane does not need to close before the logistics network is disrupted.
The route is technically open, though vessel traffic remains significantly below normal levels, and yet market behavior suggests something very different.
That distinction matters because logistics capacity is driven not only by physical access, but also by confidence.

Shipowners, charterers, insurers, banks, and cargo interests all price risk. A vessel may be able to pass through a chokepoint, but operators may still delay sailings, reroute cargo, pay higher insurance premiums, or keep tonnage elsewhere while reassessing exposure.

The consequences extend far beyond the affected waterway. Reduced tanker availability impacts freight rates. Higher risk premiums influence bunker costs and financing decisions. Equipment positioning becomes less predictable. Capacity tightens even when no formal closure exists.

The effects are no longer limited to crude oil. Refined fuel movements across Asia face growing constraints, while sanctions and payment restrictions continue to complicate trade involving Iran and counterparties in major trading markets including India and China. Geopolitical disruption should not be measured solely by whether a route is officially closed. The more important question is whether cargo can still move at a predictable cost, with acceptable risk, and with reliable access to capacity, insurance, and finance.
Once those conditions begin to deteriorate, the logistics network is already disrupted long before anyone hangs a "𝗖𝗟𝗢𝗦𝗘𝗗" sign on the map.
